newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran deadline to fire illegal aliens expires.
newsitem.headline: Iran deadline to fire illegal aliens expires.

text.p: A deadline for Iranian employers to fire an estimated one million foreign workers, mostly Afghan refugees, expired on Saturday as part of Iran's campaign to fight high unemployment.

Iran says most of the foreigners are illegal aliens, and has refused to renew residence permits for large groups of Afghans, telling them to return home or live in refugee camps. Employers were required to replace them with Iranians by January 4 or face legal consequences.

But employers and residents said they doubted the drive would be successful, as most of the low-paid workers were concentrated in sectors such as construction and agriculture where authorities had little control.
"If you visit any farm outside Tehran supplying chickens to the city, you'll see that the place is full of Afghan workers. But the authorities rarely go there," one employer said.

Employers said many state bodies themselves hired thousands of Afghans, who are generally willing to work for lower wages than Iranians. City municipalities, for example, employed large number of Afghans as street sweepers and labourers.
"It will be interesting to see if the Tehran municipality fires its own foreign workers. I think that will show how serious this new order is," a resident said.
The Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs set the deadline last month, saying most of the around one million foreigners working in the country did not hold residence or work permits.

Mostafa Musavi, a labour ministry official, told local press he expected about 100,000 jobs to open up within three months after the deadline. He said 1,000 illegal workers had been replaced by Iranians over the last month.
"Whenever Iran does not receive international aid for refugees it starts to pressure us to return home," an Afghan construction technician told Reuters.

"Iranian workers also feel threatened by Afghans because we are no longer the unskilled bunch who fled the war and came here a decade ago. Some of us have become skilled and are much in demand," he said.

A construction contractor told Reuters that most employers preferred Afghan workers because they were "more hard-working and have lower expectations. They mostly aren't trouble-makers and tend to live without their families on the sites."
He said the government clampdown was unlikely to work because Iranian labour was too expensive by comparison.
"Without Afghan workers, costs will increase as daily wages would go up 80 to 100 percent. So I'll keep my Afghan workers."

Iran, which suffers from an official unemployment rate of nearly 11 percent, is home to two million refugees -- 1.4 million from Afghanistan and 600,000 from Iraq. This makes Iran, with a population of 58 million, the world's most important host country, according to the United Nations refugee agency.
